title: nano-pixelmoe: A Mixture of Experts on Raw Pixels
author: Tatra Labs

sections.value:
Nearly every image generator in use works the same way, and it is a workaround. It does not denoise pixels; it denoises the compressed latent space of a separately trained autoencoder, because pixels were held to be too many and too redundant to denoise directly. PixelMoE (Dong et al., October 2026) throws that autoencoder away, denoises raw pixels with a transformer whose feed-forward layers are routed experts, and still reports FID 1.47 on ImageNet 256×256. Its code is "coming soon".
nano-pixelmoe is an independent version you can read in one sitting: three files, about 250 lines, and a training run that finishes on a laptop before lunch.

The claim worth testing is narrow and it is not about pixels. It is that the mixture-of-experts recipe which made large language models cheap transfers to diffusion unchanged — fine-grained experts, one always-on shared expert, top-A routing on sigmoid scores, and load balancing done by a bias rather than by a term in the loss. So the repository implements that recipe to the letter and trains it against its own dense twin: same seed, same recipe, same number of steps, and the dense FFN width chosen so that both models do within a percent of the same arithmetic per token.

```bash
python train.py --out runs/moe                # PixelMoE E32A4
python train.py --out runs/dense --experts 0  # its dense twin
python fid.py runs/moe                        # FID and IS, 10k samples
python analyze.py runs/moe -o experts.png     # the routing figure
```

CIFAR-10, class-conditional, 32×32 pixels, patch size 4, 30,000 steps at batch 128 — 77 epochs. FID and Inception score on 10,000 samples against the training set, guidance 1.5, 40 sampling steps, one RTX 5060 Laptop.

That is a tie, and I am going to call it one. A 0.30 difference in a 10,000-sample FID is noise; the dense model wins the Inception score by a similar nothing. Anyone who reports this as a win for the mixture of experts is reading their own hope. The paper's own numbers say where the win lives — Dense-B 4.40 against PixelMoE-B 2.46 — and that is at 200M+ active parameters and more than a hundred epochs of ImageNet, two orders of magnitude from a laptop.

What a laptop can settle is whether the machinery works, and the interesting half of that is load balancing. A router is free to send every token to the same expert, and left alone it does: the other thirty-one get no gradient, stay useless, and the model becomes a small dense one wearing a large coat. The standard fix is an auxiliary loss that punishes imbalance, which also pulls the router away from the experts it actually wanted. PixelMoE's recipe instead keeps a per-expert bias that is added to the scores only when picking the top A, and nudges it after every step toward uniform load. It is in no loss, it receives no gradient, and it never changes how much a chosen expert's output counts.

It works, and it works without being asked twice. Two hundred steps in, the worst layer has an expert hogging 4.7× its share. By step 1,000 the bias has it under 1.5×, and it stays between 1.24× and 1.83× for the rest of the run. The experts that balance are then free to specialise, and they do — on two different axes at once.

sections.alt: Six CIFAR-10 images above maps of which expert each patch was routed to, and a heatmap of expert use against noise level
sections.caption: From the trained run. Top: six CIFAR-10 images. Middle: the top-1 expert of every 4×4 patch in the last MoE layer, one colour per expert. Right: each expert's share of patches at twelve noise levels. Routing follows the content — the dog's body, the sky band behind the plane — and shifts with noise, with two experts taking over the last, nearly clean steps.

sections.value: That second axis is the one I did not expect. A diffusion model at t = 0.8 and the same model at t = 0.05 are doing genuinely different jobs — inventing layout versus sharpening edges — and here they end up running through different experts, which no part of the training objective asked for. The hierarchical flow matching underneath makes the split sharper still, because the two stages already divide the work by resolution.

Simplified on purpose, and worth knowing before you scale it up: timestep and class enter through AdaLN rather than as in-context tokens, the prediction head is one wide block instead of the paper's full DDT head, and the optimiser is AdamW rather than Muon. The MoE step is 1.87× slower than the dense one at equal active parameters, which is a property of my implementation and not of the method: the experts run as two batched matmuls over a padded per-expert buffer, so the padding is wasted work that a grouped-GEMM kernel would not do.
Config in model.py holds every size — width, depth, expert count, active experts, expert widths. Five tests cover routing, the matched-parameter claim, both resolutions, the sampler, and the stage transition's covariance; they run in 21 seconds.
